outcome: Not settled as of 13 October 2026, and I found no new value, bound or resolution for the tripod-packing count f(n) dated after 26 January 2024: the best lower-bound exponent (n^1.546, Gowers and Long, 2016), the exact values f(10)=32 and f(11)=38 (Östergård and Pöllänen, 2018/2019) and the small-n exact values (Szabó 2013) all predate the window, and the only in-window item is a 14 July 2026 OEIS editorial note that withdraws the a(12)–a(14) values previously attributed to Tiskin (2007) and creates no new value.
problem_asks: The statement asks for one quantity: the maximum number of tripods whose apexes can be packed into a given cube, with the tripods non-overlapping. Unpacked: (1) a quantity f(n) indexed by the size of the cube (the 'given cube'); (2) 'how many' asks for its value for each cube, i.e. the exact f(n) for every n, since no closed form is stated; (3) the statement does not itself ask for an asymptotic growth rate or for the packing density of space, although the literature's form of the question (Stein's problem) and the Wikipedia article's 'best known lower and upper bounds' concern the growth of f(n); (4) the statement contains no conjectured direction: it is a question, not an assertion. Wikipedia defines a tripod as an infinite polycube (the union of grid cubes along three positive axis-aligned rays from a shared apex); the finite version studied in the literature is the order-n tripod, the corner of an integer n×n×n cube with its three adjacent edges (3n−2 unit cubes), with the apex at a cell of the cube. Whether non-integer cube sides matter is not addressed by any source I read.

events.what_happened: W. Hamaker and S. K. Stein, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory (1984), cited in the OEIS entry A070214 and in the Wikipedia article as an early improvement on the naive bound for the tripod count. The paper was not opened; its content is known only from those two citations, which describe it only as an improvement on the naive bound.
events.delivers: Per the two secondary citations only: a bound on f(n) that improves the naive bound. The specific bound and the cube sizes it covers are not known to me.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, so far as this event goes.
events.doubts: Content not read; known only from two secondary citations.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: a bound, not a resolution.

events.what_happened: Rob Pratt, by integer programming, computed bounds on the monotonic-matrix maximum A070214, the sequence that the OEIS entry, Aronov et al. and Östergård and Pöllänen identify with the tripod count (their values agree where both are known, e.g. f(10)=32, f(11)=38): a(7)=19, 23≤a(8)≤28, 28≤a(9)≤42, 32≤a(10)≤62, with n≤6 confirmed. The OEIS gives the work's dates as 27 July to 23 August 2003 (the contribution window, not a publication date). Known from the OEIS entry only; the original is not opened.
events.revisions: OEIS entry since revised, including the 2026 note listed below.
events.delivers: Bounds on f(n) for n = 7 to 10 only, and exact values for n ≤ 6 (with K. Joy and Szabó credited for n ≤ 6 in the OEIS entry). Finite instances; no general bound.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for general n; the exact value for n = 7 to 10 is later settled by Szabó (2013) and Östergård and Pöllänen (2019) and is no longer open at those n.

machine_checked.system: Integer programming (solver not identified in the OEIS entry)

events.doubts: Known only from the OEIS entry; the original write-up was not located.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: finite bounds on the count.

events.what_happened: A. Tiskin, 'Tripods do not pack densely', COCOON 2000, Lecture Notes in Computer Science vol. 1858 (per the Wikipedia reference list and the title of a conference-version record on the SPBU portal). The paper was not opened. Secondary records (Warwick and SPBU listings) say it answers the density question negatively, which the 2007 abstract I read also states.
events.revisions: Journal version: Tiskin (2007), Discrete Mathematics, see its own event.
events.delivers: Per the title and secondary records only: the fraction of space that tripods of growing order can fill must tend to zero, so no constant-density packing exists. This concerns density, not the count for a given cube size, so it bears on the growth of f(n) only indirectly.
events.remains: The exact value of f(n) for each n; the true growth of f(n) between the known lower and upper bounds.
events.doubts: Paper not read; its content is inferred from the title and from the 2007 journal abstract that restates the same result.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: a density statement, no counterexample.

events.what_happened: A. Tiskin, 'Packing tripods: a computational approach', ALCOMFT technical report TR-03-7, June 2003 (Warwick work packages 4 and 5). The report page, read through a summarizing fetch, says the best previously known lower bound was f(n) = Ω(n^1.5235) and that computational experiments improve it to Ω(n^1.5287), with conjectures on the structure of good packings. Opened as a web page; the abstract was paraphrased by the fetch tool.
events.delivers: A lower bound f(n) = Ω(n^1.5287) for the growth of the tripod count, obtained by computer search; this moves the quantity the problem asks about, but only as an asymptotic lower bound.
events.remains: Exact f(n) for every n; the true order of growth, since the upper bound is far above this lower bound.
events.doubts: Technical report, not peer reviewed in the form I read. Superseded as the best lower bound by Gowers and Long (2016), since n^1.546 exceeds n^1.5287.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: a lower bound on the count's growth.
events.object: A computer-found family of tripod packings giving the exponent 1.5287; the explicit packings were not read.

events.what_happened: A. Tiskin, 'Packing tripods: narrowing the density gap', Discrete Mathematics 307(16) (2007) 1973–1981, DOI 10.1016/j.disc.2004.12.028. Warwick metadata: first presented at ECCG 2003 (Prague, 8–12 September 2003), submitted 8 September 2003, accepted 12 December 2004, published 28 July 2007. The abstract, read through a fetch summary with quotation limits, states that the fraction of space that can be filled with tripods must be infinitely small as the order grows; that the asymptotic lower bound on packing density is improved; and that computational results are given for low-order packings. Wikipedia and the OEIS entry attribute the o(n²) upper bound on f(n) to this work.
events.revisions: Journal publication 28 July 2007. The ECCG 2003 presentation is the earliest public appearance I found; I could not confirm from the record whether it contained the full argument.
events.delivers: (i) The fraction of space fillable by tripods tends to zero as the order grows, i.e. no constant-density packing. (ii) An improved asymptotic lower bound on packing density, exponent not read. (iii) Computational small-n results, which the OEIS entry later partly withdraws (see the 2026 event). (iv) Per Wikipedia and OEIS, an upper bound f(n) = o(n²). None of these gives the exact count for a given n.
events.remains: Exact f(n) for n ≥ 10 except where later established; the true growth exponent between the lower bounds and the upper bound.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted 12 December 2004 and published 2007 (per Warwick metadata)

events.doubts: (1) Wikipedia says that Tiskin's suggested polylogarithmic improvement of the upper bound 'appears to be a mistake'; the summary I read does not say which paper the suggestion is in, so I cannot say whether this one. (2) The OEIS 2026 note says Tiskin's values for n = 12 to 14 are for 3-symmetric packings only, so the computational small-n claims are not general maxima. (3) The date of the first public version is uncertain (see revisions).
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: a density statement (no constant-density packing), and an upper bound on f(n) of order o(n²). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: S. Szabó, 'Monotonic matrices and clique search in graphs', Annales Universitatis Scientiarum Budapestinensis, Sectio Computatorica 41 (2013) 307–322. Reformulates the problem as the maximum number of filled cells in an n×n monotonic matrix and determines that maximum for 7 ≤ n ≤ 9, by partly theoretical arguments and partly computer-aided exhaustive search (per the abstract excerpt). The OEIS reading gives 19, 23, 28 for n = 7, 8, 9. The paper's full text was not opened.
events.delivers: Exact values of the monotonic-matrix maximum, which Östergård and Pöllänen identify with f(n), for 7 ≤ n ≤ 9. Finite instances only.
events.remains: f(n) for n ≥ 10, as Östergård and Pöllänen have since taken n = 10 and 11; f(n) for n ≥ 12 in general.

checked_by.who: Annales Universitatis Scientiarum Budapestinensis, Sectio Computatorica (referees)

machine_checked.system: Computer-aided exhaustive search (program not identified in the abstract excerpt)

events.doubts: Full text not read; the value-to-n mapping for 7–9 comes from my reading of the OEIS sequence, not a quote from the paper.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: exact finite values only.

events.what_happened: B. Aronov, V. Dujmović, P. Morin, A. Ooms and L. F. Schultz Xavier da Silveira, 'More Turán-type theorems for triangles in convex point sets', arXiv 1706.10193 (v1 30 June 2017; v2 11 September 2018; v3 7 December 2018, whose comments say it corrects one theorem statement); Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 26(1) (2019) #P1.8. The arXiv abstract was read: the eight ways two triangles can interact give 256 Turán-type questions; nearly tight bounds (within a log n factor) are proved for 248; the remaining 8 'are all asymptotically equivalent to Stein's longstanding tripod packing problem'. Section 1.2 (read in an HTML rendering) lists the same problem as 'monotone matrices, tripod packing, and 2-comparable triples'.
events.revisions: v2 11 Sep 2018; v3 7 Dec 2018 corrects one theorem statement (not identified); journal EJC 26(1) 2019 #P1.8.
events.delivers: Establishes that eight convex-triangle Turán-type questions are asymptotically equivalent to the tripod problem, and gives log-factor-tight bounds for the other 248. It is a reformulation: it does not by itself change any bound on the tripod count f(n).
events.remains: The tripod problem itself: exact f(n) for every n, and the growth of f(n).
events.doubts: The equivalence is asymptotic, i.e. stated up to a log factor for the 8 cases; it is not an exact identity of counts. The v3 correction to one theorem statement is not identified in what I read.
events.direction: Neutral: a reformulation that ties the Turán-type problem to tripod packing; it cuts neither way on f(n).
people: Luís Fernando Schultz Xavier da Silveira

events.what_happened: W. T. Gowers and J. Long, 'The length of an s-increasing sequence of r-tuples', arXiv 1609.08688 (v1 27 September 2016; v2 2 November 2016, which corrects an error in v1 about transitive sets); Combinatorics, Probability and Computing (2021), per the Wikipedia reference list and Aronov et al. The abstract was read: a problem of Po-Shen Loh about 2-increasing sequences of triples, a log* improvement over the trivial n² bound using the triangle removal lemma, and a simple n^(3/2) construction. Theorem 1.14, read in an HTML rendering summarized by the fetch tool: for arbitrarily large n there are 2-comparable sets of triples of size at least n^1.546, the exponent being 3α with α between 0.5154 and 0.5155. Per Aronov et al. (Section 1.2) 2-comparable triples are the tripod problem in another guise, so this is a tripod lower bound of order n^1.546 (Wikipedia states it directly).
events.revisions: v2 2 Nov 2016 corrects an error in v1 about transitive sets; published CPC 2021 (per Wikipedia and Aronov et al.; journal page not opened).
events.delivers: A lower bound on the tripod count of order n^1.546 for large n, through the 2-comparable-triples formulation, which supersedes the Tiskin 2003 exponent 1.5287. Also an upper-bound statement for the 2-increasing quantity: n²/2^Ω(log* n) (Prop. 1.6 in the summary read). Whether that upper bound transfers to the 2-comparable/tripod quantity is unclear from what I read (see doubts). Neither bound settles the exact values.
events.remains: Exact f(n) for every n; the gap between n^1.546 and the upper bound.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published 2021 (per Wikipedia and Aronov et al.); journal record not opened

events.directly_checkable: The lower-bound construction is a finite combinatorial object for each n, checkable for small n by computer; I did not check any instance.
events.doubts: (1) The abstract does not mention tripods, Stein, packing or monotone matrices; the tripod link is via the Aronov et al. equivalence and Wikipedia. (2) The exponent 1.546 is read from a summarized HTML rendering, not the PDF text, which the fetch tool could not read. (3) v1 contained an error, corrected in v2; I could not tell whether Theorem 1.14 changed. (4) The sources disagree on which quantity the log* upper bound concerns: the fetch summary says Proposition 1.6 is for the 2-increasing quantity F(n) and that the argument does not improve the 2-comparable Problem 1.9, while Aronov et al. (Table 2) and Wikipedia list n²/2^Ω(log* n) for tripods.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem as a bound: it shows the simple n^(3/2) construction is not the truth for the tripod count; no counterexample to any claimed value.
events.object: A construction, for arbitrarily large n, of 2-comparable sets of triples in a cube of side n of size at least n^1.546 (per the summary read); per Aronov et al. these correspond to tripod packings of the same size. Whether the construction is explicit or non-constructive was not established from what I read.

events.what_happened: P. R. J. Östergård and A. Pöllänen, 'New results on tripod packings', Discrete & Computational Geometry 61(2) (2019) 271–284, DOI 10.1007/s00454-018-0012-2 (early online 18 June 2018, per the Aalto record). The Aalto abstract summary, read: f(n) is studied in the maximum-clique framework; f(10) = 32 and f(11) = 38 are obtained computationally (f(n) was previously known only for n ≤ 9); prescribing symmetries gives constructive lower bounds on f(n) for n ≤ 26; a conjecture that f(n) is always attained by a packing with an order-3 symmetry rotating the cube about an axis through two opposite vertices is disproved. The companion Zenodo dataset (10.5281/zenodo.1230276, deposited 26 April 2018, CC-BY-4.0) is said to prove the lower bounds in Table 5. The Springer article and the Zenodo record were not opened (redirect to login and HTTP 504).
events.revisions: Early online 18 June 2018; print DCG 61(2) 2019 (15 March 2019 per the Aalto record). Dataset deposited 26 April 2018.
events.delivers: Exact values f(10) = 32 and f(11) = 38, and constructive lower bounds for f(n) at n ≤ 26 by symmetry-restricted packings; the order-3 symmetry conjecture is disproved. Finite results, and lower bounds for n ≥ 12 that are not shown to be optimal.
events.remains: Exact f(n) for n ≥ 12; the growth of f(n); whether the symmetry-restricted lower bounds are optimal.

machine_checked.system: Maximum-clique computations (software not identified in sources read); packings supplied as a Zenodo dataset

events.directly_checkable: The explicit packings for f(10) and f(11) and the symmetric packings for n ≤ 26 are in the Zenodo dataset (not opened). Each packing can be checked for disjointness by computer; the upper values rest on the clique search.
events.doubts: No independent reproduction found in the sources I read. The dataset and the full table were not read.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: exact finite values and constructive lower bounds; no counterexample to a claimed bound.
events.object: Explicit packings of tripods in n×n×n cubes: 32 tripods for n = 10 and 38 for n = 11, which the paper's clique search shows to be maximal; plus symmetric packings for n ≤ 26. Packings are explicit (computer-found); the exactness rests on the exhaustive clique computation.

events.what_happened: An OEIS editorial note by Andrei Zabolotskii, dated 14 July 2026, removes the terms a(12) to a(14) from the Extensions of A070214 (the monotonic-matrix maximum, which matches f(n) where both are known). The note says that the values Tiskin (2007) gave for these n are for 3-symmetric packings only. The current OEIS entry lists terms only up to n = 11, although an older cached search snippet still listed 43, 49, 55 for n = 12 to 14. Read through a summarizing fetch of the OEIS page; the note was not read verbatim.
events.revisions: OEIS A070214 edited 14 Jul 2026 (removal of a(12)–a(14)); an earlier revision dated 9 Jul 2020 corrected a(11).
events.delivers: No new value. It withdraws the attribution to the general problem of a(12) = 43, a(13) = 49 and a(14) = 55 from the Tiskin (2007) extensions, on the ground that they are restricted to 3-symmetric packings.
events.doubts: An editorial note on an OEIS entry, not a referee check. I did not verify the 3-symmetric claim against Tiskin's paper.

withdrawn.what: The OEIS terms a(12)=43, a(13)=49, a(14)=55 of A070214, previously attributed to Tiskin (2007) as extensions of the sequence

events.direction: Neutral to the problem's answer: it narrows what is established for f(n) at n = 12 to 14.

disputes.summary: Posing date of Stein's problem: 1967 (Wikipedia, citing Stein's 'Factoring by subsets'), 1984 (Tiskin 2007 as recorded by Warwick and SPBU), 1994 (Stein and Szabó, per the Tiskin 2003 report and the COCOON 2000 title). Wikipedia also cites Stein and Szabó's 1994 book 'Algebra and Tiling'. No result depends on the posing date, so this is not a priority dispute.
Wikipedia says that Tiskin's suggested polylogarithmic improvement of the packing-number upper bound 'appears to be a mistake'. The paper and the error are not identified in the summary I read.

OEIS (14 July 2026) withdraws the a(12)–a(14) values attributed to Tiskin (2007), saying they are for 3-symmetric packings only. I did not check Tiskin's paper for whether it claimed general maxima at those n; the attribution question remains open on my reading.

Whether the log* upper bound n²/2^Ω(log* n) applies to the tripod (2-comparable) quantity or only to the 2-increasing quantity F(n). Gowers and Long (Prop. 1.6, per a summary) state it for F(n); Aronov et al. (Table 2) and Wikipedia list it for tripods.

summary: Across 57 web searches and about 25 opened pages (plus several searches that returned only the titles of unopened papers), I found no event dated after 26 January 2024 that moves a bound on f(n), the largest number of tripods that pack into an n×n×n cube, nor any new exact value. The state of the record: exact values f(n) are known for n ≤ 11 (small n from Pratt's integer-programming bounds and Szabó 2013; f(10)=32 and f(11)=38 from Östergård and Pöllänen, 2018/2019). The best lower bound I can attribute is n^1.546, from Gowers and Long (arXiv 2016, CPC 2021), via Theorem 1.14 on 2-comparable triples, which Aronov et al. (2017/2019) show is the tripod problem in another formulation; this supersedes Tiskin's 2003 exponent 1.5287. The upper bound is o(n²) (Tiskin 2007), with n²/2^Ω(log* n) attributed to the problem by Wikipedia and Aronov et al. The Wikipedia article (last edited 22 June 2026, as the fetch summary reports) cites nothing later than the 2021 journal publication of Gowers and Long, and I found no later preprint, journal paper, blog, Lean project, or AI-lab announcement on this problem. The one in-window item is the OEIS editorial note of 14 July 2026 by Andrei Zabolotskii, which removes the a(12)–a(14) values from the sequence's extensions as 3-symmetric-only and creates no new value. Close calls: (a) I include the 2026 OEIS note as an event because it changes which values are attributed to the problem, though it proves nothing; (b) the n^1.546 bound counts as a bound on this problem only through the Aronov et al. equivalence, which the Gowers–Long abstract does not state, and I read that theorem through a summarizing fetch rather than the PDF; (c) the log* upper bound's applicability to the tripod quantity is ambiguous across sources. AI: no AI system was credited with any tripod-packing result in any source I found. I searched for AI involvement with the problem's name, Stein, tripods, monotone matrices and 2-comparable triples; checked the OpenAI Astra results (the primary page returned 403; two secondary accounts omit tripods), the AlphaEvolve packing paper (visible text does not mention tripods; section 6.19 'Packing problems' was truncated), the Epoch FrontierMath Open Problems list (10 of 49 items visible, none tripod-related), and the Google, Anthropic and OpenAI results found in search, none of which mention tripods. Every event therefore has ai.none_found true. Coverage is limited: the niche combinatorics literature is thinly indexed by this search tool, and several primary sources (Springer, Zenodo, OpenAI, both Gowers–Long and Aronov PDFs) could not be read directly.
competing_reading: The strongest case for a different reading: the 1.546 exponent is credited only through the Aronov et al. equivalence, which is asymptotic up to log factors, and the Gowers–Long abstract never mentions tripods, so the tripod problem's lower bound could be read as still n^1.5287 (Tiskin 2003) with the 1.546 figure living in a neighbouring problem. The reverse reading: the 2026 OEIS note withdraws values and so is a regression on the problem's known small-n frontier, not merely an attribution clean-up, which would make the record's status for n = 12 to 14 less than the older sources implied. A third reading holds that nothing happened in the window at all, and that the OEIS note should be discounted as an editorial correction rather than an event.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Gowers and Long (arXiv 1609.08688) for Theorem 1.14 and Proposition 1.6, specifically whether the stated bounds are for the 2-comparable set quantity used for tripods and whether v1 and v2 agree. (2) The Östergård–Pöllänen Table 5 and the Zenodo dataset, to confirm the symmetric lower bounds and whether any n ≥ 12 value is claimed as exact. (3) The full text of the 14 July 2026 OEIS note and Tiskin 2007's statements for n ≥ 12. (4) The remaining 39 items of Epoch's FrontierMath Open Problems list, and the openai.com Astra page, to rule out a tripod item there. (5) The Aronov et al. v3 correction to one theorem statement, to see whether it touches the equivalence.
